Keywords: Lakhmids Imru al-Qays II Artisan Forges
RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Lakhmids in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Al-Hirah (White Palaces), merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Lakhmids was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Al-Hirah (White Palaces), cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Camel drivers lead their strings through the market at Al-Hirah, the bells on their harnesses ringing over the crowd. A guard walks beside the loads with a club at his belt, watching the crowd for thieves. His pay is a few silver coins and a share of the tolls, and he hopes the caravans keep arriving through the desert.

Keeping the palace accounts at Al-Hirah, the steward measures the tolls on silk, spice, and dates owed to the king. The caravans from the desert pay in kind, and the best goods are reserved for the court. He records each merchant who delays payment, because the Nasrid kings will ask for those names.
